lesson.intro: Two kinds of question live in this topic, and the test likes to put them side by side. The first is a \emph{nonlinear system}: a line meeting a parabola or a circle, where the work is to substitute one equation into the other and solve the quadratic that appears. The second is \emph{function transformation}: reading $f(x-3)$, $-f(x)$ or $2f(x)$ and knowing exactly how the picture moves. Both reward the same habit --- decide what is happening to the input and what is happening to the output, then do the algebra one step at a time.

blocks.title: Solving a nonlinear system by substitution
blocks.body: A system is a pair of conditions that must hold at the same point. When one equation is already solved for $y$, put that expression into the other equation. Every $y$ disappears and a single equation in $x$ is left --- almost always a quadratic.\\[4pt] For $y=x^{2}-3x+5$ and $y=x+2$: substitute to get $x^{2}-3x+5=x+2$, collect everything on one side, $x^{2}-4x+3=0$, and factor, $(x-1)(x-3)=0$. The $x$-coordinates are $1$ and $3$. \emph{Finish the job}: put each back into the line to get $y=3$ and $y=5$, so the solutions are $(1,3)$ and $(3,5)$. A system with two intersection points has two solutions, and a question asking for a sum of coordinates wants both of them.

blocks.title: Two equations become one equation
blocks.body: Whatever the curves are, the goal never changes: eliminate a variable. With a circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=r^{2}$ and a line, substitute the line's $y$ into the circle. With a circle and a parabola $y=x^{2}+k$, it is often faster to eliminate $x^{2}$ instead, since $x^{2}=y-k$ turns the circle equation into a quadratic in $y$. Then remember that one $y$-value can correspond to two $x$-values: if $x^{2}=7$, that is two points, but if $x^{2}=0$, it is only one.

blocks.title: How many times do the graphs meet?
blocks.body: Once the system has been reduced to $ax^{2}+bx+c=0$, the number of intersection points is the number of \emph{real} solutions, and the discriminant $b^{2}-4ac$ answers that without any solving:\\[4pt] $b^{2}-4ac>0$: two intersection points. $\;b^{2}-4ac=0$: one point, and the line is \emph{tangent} to the curve. $\;b^{2}-4ac<0$: the graphs never meet.\\[4pt] Every ``for what value of $c$ is the line tangent to the curve'' question is this identity read backwards: set the discriminant equal to zero and solve for the parameter.

blocks.title: The transformation table
blocks.body: Let $k>0$ and let $f$ be any function.\\[4pt] $f(x)+k$ --- shift \textbf{up} $k$. \quad $f(x)-k$ --- shift \textbf{down} $k$.\\ $f(x+k)$ --- shift \textbf{left} $k$. \quad $f(x-k)$ --- shift \textbf{right} $k$.\\ $-f(x)$ --- reflect across the $\boldsymbol{x}$\textbf{-axis}. \quad $f(-x)$ --- reflect across the $\boldsymbol{y}$\textbf{-axis}.\\ $af(x)$ with $a>1$ --- vertical \textbf{stretch} by $a$; with $0<a<1$ --- vertical \textbf{shrink}.\\ $f(bx)$ with $b>1$ --- horizontal \textbf{compression} by $b$; with $0<b<1$ --- horizontal \textbf{stretch}.\\[4pt] One rule organises the whole table: changes \emph{outside} the parentheses act on $y$ and behave as written; changes \emph{inside} act on $x$ and behave in reverse.

blocks.title: The shift inside the parentheses goes the wrong way
blocks.body: $f(x-3)$ shifts the graph $3$ units \textbf{right}, not left, and $f(x+6)$ shifts it $6$ units \textbf{left}. The minus sign looks like ``go negative'', which is why this is the single most missed transformation on the test.\\[4pt] Never argue from the sign --- test a point. If $g(x)=f(x-3)$, then $g(3)=f(0)$: the output $f$ produced at $x=0$ now appears at $x=3$, so the picture moved to the right. The same check settles $f(2x)$: if $f$ has an $x$-intercept at $6$, then $f(2x)=0$ needs $2x=6$, so the new intercept is at $x=3$ --- the graph was squeezed toward the $y$-axis, not stretched away from it.

blocks.title: Stretches act on one variable only
blocks.body: $3f(x)$ multiplies every \emph{output} by $3$: the point $(2,5)$ becomes $(2,15)$, and the $x$-coordinate does not budge. $f(3x)$ multiplies every \emph{input} by $3$: the point $(6,5)$ becomes $(2,5)$, and the $y$-coordinate does not budge. Mixing these up --- or adding $3$ where the rule says multiply --- accounts for most wrong answers on stretch questions.

blocks.title: Work outside-in, and use a single point
blocks.body: For a compound transformation such as $y=-2f(x+1)-3$, name the pieces in order: inside first ($1$ unit left), then the stretch and reflection ($\times(-2)$: flip across the $x$-axis and stretch vertically by $2$), then the vertical shift ($3$ down).\\[4pt] When a graph or a table is given, do not transform the whole picture --- transform one point you can read exactly, usually a vertex or an intercept, and see which choice agrees. And when a question gives a table, remember that the inside change tells you \emph{which row to read} and the outside change tells you \emph{what to do with the number you read}.

blocks.title: Worked example 1 --- a line and a parabola
blocks.body: \textbf{The graphs of $y=x^{2}-4x+7$ and $y=2x-1$ intersect at two points. What is the sum of the $y$-coordinates of those points?}\\[4pt] Substitute the line into the parabola: $x^{2}-4x+7=2x-1$. Bring everything to one side: $x^{2}-6x+8=0$, which factors as $(x-2)(x-4)=0$, so $x=2$ and $x=4$.\\[4pt] The question asks for $y$-coordinates, so use the line (it is the easier equation): $y=2(2)-1=3$ and $y=2(4)-1=7$. The sum is $3+7=10$.\\[4pt] \emph{Why this order:} substituting the \emph{linear} expression is what keeps the algebra to a single quadratic, and returning to the \emph{linear} equation at the end keeps the arithmetic to one multiplication. Stopping at $x=2,4$ and answering $6$ is the classic incomplete answer.

blocks.title: Worked example 2 --- tangency and the discriminant
blocks.body: \textbf{For what value of $c$ is the line $y=6x+c$ tangent to the parabola $y=x^{2}+2x+5$?}\\[4pt] Substitute: $x^{2}+2x+5=6x+c$, so $x^{2}-4x+(5-c)=0$. Tangent means the two intersection points have merged into one, so this quadratic has exactly one real root and its discriminant is zero:\\[4pt] $(-4)^{2}-4(1)(5-c)=0 \;\Rightarrow\; 16-20+4c=0 \;\Rightarrow\; c=1$.\\[4pt] \emph{Check:} with $c=1$ the equation is $x^{2}-4x+4=(x-2)^{2}=0$, a repeated root at $x=2$ --- a single point of contact, as tangency requires. Note the sign work in $5-c$: carrying $c$ across the equals sign incorrectly is where this problem is normally lost.

blocks.title: Worked example 3 --- reading a transformed function from a table
blocks.body: \textbf{The table below gives values of $f$. If $g(x)=-2f(x-1)+4$, what is $g(3)$?}\\[4pt] \begin{center}\renewcommand{\arraystretch}{1.2}\begin{tabular}{@{}c|cccc@{}} $x$ & $1$ & $2$ & $3$ & $4$ \\ \midrule $f(x)$ & $0$ & $5$ & $-2$ & $7$ \end{tabular}\end{center} Inside first: $g(3)$ requires $f(3-1)=f(2)$, and the table gives $f(2)=5$. Now apply the outside operations in order: multiply by $-2$ to get $-10$, then add $4$ to get $-6$. So $g(3)=-6$.\\[4pt] \emph{Why the inside comes first:} $x-1$ decides which input $f$ receives, and that has to be settled before $f$ can produce a number at all. Reading $f(3)=-2$ (ignoring the shift) gives $8$, and reading $f(4)=7$ (shifting the wrong way) gives $-10$ --- both appear as answer choices on the real test.

problems.stem: The graph of $y=x^{2}$ is shifted $5$ units up in the $xy$-plane. Which equation represents the resulting graph?
problems.solution: Adding a constant \emph{outside} the function changes the output, so every point moves straight up: $y=x^{2}+5$. The choices with $5$ inside the parentheses move the graph sideways, not up.
steps: A shift up adds to the output: replace $y$ by $y-5$, i.e. $y=x^{2}+5$.
Check the vertex: $(0,0)$ moves to $(0,5)$, and $y=0^{2}+5=5$.
problems.verify: result = "$y=x^{2}+5$"

problems.stem: The function $g$ is defined by $g(x)=f(x-3)$. Which of the following describes the graph of $y=g(x)$ compared with the graph of $y=f(x)$?
choices: The graph of $f$ shifted $3$ units to the left.
The graph of $f$ shifted $3$ units to the right.
The graph of $f$ shifted $3$ units up.
The graph of $f$ shifted $3$ units down.
problems.solution: A change inside the parentheses moves the graph horizontally, and it moves it the \emph{opposite} way from the sign you see. To get the same output that $f$ gave at some input, $g$ needs an $x$ that is $3$ larger, so every point slides $3$ units right.
steps: The change $x-3$ is inside the function, so the shift is horizontal.
$g(3)=f(0)$: the point that $f$ had at $x=0$ now sits at $x=3$.
So the graph moves $3$ units to the right.
problems.verify: result = "The graph of $f$ shifted $3$ units to the right."

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the graphs of $y=2x$ and $y=x^{2}-3$ intersect at two points. What is the greatest $x$-coordinate of an intersection point?
problems.solution: Two graphs meet where their $y$-values agree, so setting the two expressions equal turns the system into a single quadratic equation in $x$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
result = max(solve(x**2 - 2*x - 3, x))

problems.stem: The graph of $y=f(x)$ is reflected across the $x$-axis. Which equation represents the reflected graph?
choices: $y=\lvert f(x)\rvert$
problems.solution: Reflecting across the $x$-axis flips the sign of every output, which is a change on the outside: $y=-f(x)$. Changing the sign of the input instead, $f(-x)$, would flip the graph left-to-right.
steps: A reflection across the $x$-axis sends $(x,y)$ to $(x,-y)$.
The $x$-values are untouched, so the negative sign goes outside: $y=-f(x)$.
problems.verify: result = "$y=-f(x)$"

problems.stem: The graph of $y=3f(x)$ is obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by which transformation?
choices: A shift of $3$ units up.
A horizontal stretch by a factor of $3$.
A vertical stretch by a factor of $3$.
A horizontal compression by a factor of $3$.
problems.solution: Multiplying the whole function by $3$ triples every output while leaving every input alone, so the graph is pulled away from the $x$-axis: a vertical stretch by a factor of $3$.
steps: The factor $3$ multiplies the output, not the input.
That is a vertical stretch by a factor of $3$.
problems.verify: result = "A vertical stretch by a factor of $3$."

problems.stem: The graphs of $y=x^{2}$ and $y=x+6$ intersect at two points in the $xy$-plane. What is the sum of the $y$-coordinates of those two points?
problems.solution: Solve for the $x$-coordinates first, then feed each one back into either equation. A common slip is to stop after finding the $x$-values, or to report only one of the two points.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
xs = solve(x**2 - (x + 6), x)
result = sum([v**2 for v in xs])

problems.stem: How many points of intersection do the graphs of $y=x^{2}+1$ and $y=x-2$ have in the $xy$-plane?
problems.solution: The number of intersection points is the number of real solutions of the combined equation, and the discriminant settles that without solving anything.
steps: A negative discriminant means no real solutions, so the graphs never meet.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x', real=True)
result = len(solve(x**2 + 1 - (x - 2), x))

problems.stem: $$y=x^{2}-4x+7$$ $$y=2x-1$$ Which ordered pair $(x,y)$ is a solution to the system of equations above?
problems.solution: Substituting the line into the parabola is the whole method: it removes $y$ and leaves a quadratic in $x$. A point must satisfy \emph{both} equations, so always finish by computing the matching $y$.
steps: $(2,3)$ is one of the two solutions.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
xs = sorted(solve(x**2 - 4*x + 7 - (2*x - 1), x))
a = xs[0]
result = (a, 2*a - 1)

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the line $y=4x+c$ is tangent to the parabola $y=x^{2}$, where $c$ is a constant. What is the value of $c$?
problems.solution: Tangent means the line touches the curve exactly once, so the quadratic you get after substituting must have exactly one real solution --- its discriminant is zero.
steps: One solution means the discriminant is $0$: $(-4)^{2}-4(1)(-c)=0$.
problems.verify:
c = symbols('c')
result = solve(16 + 4*c, c)[0]

problems.stem: The system of equations $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$ and $y=x+1$ has two solutions in the $xy$-plane. What is the greatest $y$-coordinate of a solution?
problems.solution: A circle and a line are handled exactly like a parabola and a line: substitute the linear equation into the other one. The quadratic that appears has two roots, and each root produces its own $y$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
xs = solve(x**2 + (x + 1)**2 - 25, x)
result = max([v + 1 for v in xs])

problems.solution: Evaluating a transformed function is a substitution, not a guess: $g(1)$ means $f$ evaluated at $1+2=3$. Reading $f(1)$ or $f(-1)$ instead is the usual error, and the table is built so both wrong readings are available.

problems.stem: The graph of $y=x^{2}$ is transformed to produce the graph of $y=(x+4)^{2}-3$. Which of the following describes the transformation?
choices: A shift $4$ units to the right and $3$ units down.
A shift $4$ units to the right and $3$ units up.
A shift $4$ units to the left and $3$ units down.
A shift $4$ units to the left and $3$ units up.
problems.solution: Read the two changes separately. The $+4$ sits inside the square, so it is horizontal and it moves the graph the opposite way: $4$ units left. The $-3$ sits outside, so it means exactly what it says: $3$ units down.
steps: $x+4$ inside the square shifts the graph $4$ units \emph{left}, since the vertex needs $x+4=0$, i.e. $x=-4$.
$-3$ outside subtracts $3$ from every output: $3$ units down.
problems.verify: result = "A shift $4$ units to the left and $3$ units down."

problems.stem: The point $(2,5)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x)$. The graph of $y=3f(x)$ passes through the point $(2,k)$. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: A vertical stretch multiplies the $y$-coordinate and leaves the $x$-coordinate alone, so $(2,5)$ becomes $(2,15)$. Adding $3$ instead of multiplying, or dividing by $3$, are the two mistakes this question is built to catch.
problems.verify: result = 3*5

problems.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x^{2}-6x$, and $g(x)=f(-x)$. Which expression is equivalent to $g(x)$?
problems.solution: Replacing $x$ by $-x$ reflects the graph across the $y$-axis. Do it algebraically: every $x$ in the formula becomes $-x$, so the even-power term is unchanged and the odd-power term flips sign.
problems.verify: result = "$x^{2}+6x$"

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the graph of $y=-x^{2}+6x$ intersects the line $y=5$ at two points. What is the positive difference between the $x$-coordinates of those two points?
problems.solution: A horizontal line makes the substitution trivial: set the quadratic equal to $5$ and solve. The two roots are the $x$-coordinates, and their difference is what the question asks for.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
xs = solve(-x**2 + 6*x - 5, x)
result = max(xs) - min(xs)

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the line $y=mx-4$ is tangent to the graph of $y=x^{2}$, where $m$ is a positive constant. What is the value of $m$?
problems.solution: Tangency is a discriminant question in disguise. Substituting gives a quadratic whose discriminant must be zero; that produces $m^{2}=16$, and the condition $m>0$ picks the root.
problems.verify:
m = symbols('m')
result = max(solve(m**2 - 16, m))

problems.stem: The solutions to the system $y=x^{2}-2x-3$ and $y=2x+2$ are $(x_{1},y_{1})$ and $(x_{2},y_{2})$. What is the value of $y_{1}+y_{2}$?
problems.solution: Find both $x$-values, then convert each to a $y$-value with the easier of the two equations --- the line. Adding the $x$-values instead of the $y$-values is the trap here.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
xs = solve(x**2 - 2*x - 3 - (2*x + 2), x)
result = sum([2*v + 2 for v in xs])

problems.stem: The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown, where $f(x)=x^{2}-4$. The function $g$ is defined by $g(x)=f(x+3)$. What is the vertex of the graph of $y=g(x)$?
problems.solution: The vertex of $f$ is at $(0,-4)$. Since the $+3$ is inside the function, the graph slides horizontally, and it slides $3$ units \emph{left}, carrying the vertex to $(-3,-4)$. The height is untouched because nothing was added outside.
steps: From the graph, the vertex of $f$ is $(0,-4)$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
h = (x + 3)**2 - 4
xv = solve(sp.diff(h, x), x)[0]
result = (xv, h.subs(x, xv))

problems.stem: The minimum value of the function $f$ is $-3$, and it occurs at $x=1$. The function $g$ is defined by $g(x)=-2f(x)$. What is the maximum value of $g$?
problems.solution: The factor $-2$ does two things at once: the negative sign flips the graph across the $x$-axis, so a minimum becomes a maximum, and the $2$ doubles the distance from the axis. So the least output $-3$ becomes the greatest output $6$.
steps: Multiplying by $-1$ turns the minimum of $f$ into a maximum of $g$.
So the maximum value of $g$ is $6$, still at $x=1$.
problems.verify: result = -2*(-3)

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the line $y=2x+c$ is tangent to the circle $x^{2}+y^{2}=45$, where $c$ is a positive constant. What is the value of $c$?
problems.solution: Tangency to a circle works the same way as tangency to a parabola: substitute, collect a quadratic in $x$, and force the discriminant to zero so the two intersection points collapse into one.
problems.verify:
c = symbols('c')
result = max(solve(-4*c**2 + 900, c))

problems.stem: The graph of $y=f(x)$ is first shifted $2$ units to the right and then reflected across the $x$-axis. Which equation represents the resulting graph?
problems.solution: Handle the two steps in order. The shift right $2$ replaces $x$ by $x-2$, giving $y=f(x-2)$; reflecting that across the $x$-axis negates the whole output, giving $y=-f(x-2)$. The negative sign never reaches inside the parentheses.
steps: Reflect across the $x$-axis: negate the output.
problems.verify: result = "$y=-f(x-2)$"

problems.stem: The graph of $y=f(x)$ has an $x$-intercept at $x=6$. The function $g$ is defined by $g(x)=f(2x)$. At what value of $x$ does the graph of $y=g(x)$ have an $x$-intercept?
problems.solution: A factor multiplying $x$ inside the function compresses the graph horizontally: to make the inside equal $6$, the new input only has to be half as large. Multiplying by $2$ instead of dividing is the standard error.
steps: $f$ is zero when its input is $6$, so $2x=6$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
result = solve(2*x - 6, x)[0]

problems.stem: The function $h$ is defined by $h(x)=f(x+6)$. Which of the following describes the graph of $y=h(x)$ compared with the graph of $y=f(x)$?
choices: The graph of $f$ shifted $6$ units to the left.
The graph of $f$ shifted $6$ units to the right.
The graph of $f$ shifted $6$ units up.
The graph of $f$ shifted $6$ units down.
problems.solution: A constant added inside the parentheses shifts the graph horizontally in the direction opposite to its sign. Here $h(-6)=f(0)$, so the point $f$ had at $x=0$ now appears at $x=-6$: the graph moves $6$ units left.
steps: $x+6$ is inside the function, so the shift is horizontal.
The graph shifts $6$ units to the left.
problems.verify: result = "The graph of $f$ shifted $6$ units to the left."

problems.stem: The graphs of $y=x^{2}+3x$ and $y=x+8$ intersect at two points in the $xy$-plane. What is the greater of the two $x$-coordinates?
problems.solution: Setting the two expressions equal eliminates $y$ and leaves a quadratic. Both roots are $x$-coordinates of genuine intersection points, so the question is only asking which one is larger.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
result = max(solve(x**2 + 3*x - (x + 8), x))

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, how many points does the graph of $y=x^{2}-4$ have in common with the line $y=-4$?
problems.solution: The line $y=-4$ passes exactly through the vertex of the parabola, so it touches the curve once instead of cutting it twice. Algebraically, the combined equation $x^{2}=0$ has a single (repeated) root.
steps: The only solution is $x=0$, so the graphs meet at exactly one point.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x', real=True)
result = len(solve(x**2 - 4 + 4, x))

problems.stem: How does the graph of $y=f(x)-7$ compare with the graph of $y=f(x)$?
choices: It is shifted $7$ units to the left.
It is shifted $7$ units to the right.
It is shifted $7$ units up.
It is shifted $7$ units down.
problems.solution: Subtracting $7$ outside the function lowers every output by $7$, so the whole graph slides straight down. Only changes inside the parentheses move a graph sideways.
steps: The $-7$ is applied to the output, not the input.
problems.verify: result = "It is shifted $7$ units down."

problems.stem: The point $(-3,8)$ lies on the graph of $y=f(x)$. The graph of $y=f(x)+5$ passes through the point $(-3,k)$. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: Adding $5$ outside the function raises the output at every input, and it never touches the $x$-coordinate. So the point at $x=-3$ keeps its position horizontally and climbs $5$ units.
steps: The new function value at $x=-3$ is $f(-3)+5$.
problems.verify: result = 8 + 5

problems.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x^{3}-2x$, and $h(x)=f(-x)$. Which expression is equivalent to $h(x)$?
problems.solution: Substitute $-x$ everywhere: the odd power flips sign and so does the $-2x$ term. The result, $-x^{3}+2x$, is the mirror image of $f$ across the $y$-axis.
problems.verify: result = "$-x^{3}+2x$"

problems.stem: The graph of $y=\frac{1}{2}f(x)$ is obtained from the graph of $y=f(x)$ by which transformation?
choices: A horizontal compression by a factor of $2$.
A horizontal stretch by a factor of $2$.
A shift down $\frac{1}{2}$ unit.
A vertical shrink by a factor of $\frac{1}{2}$.
problems.solution: The factor $\frac{1}{2}$ multiplies the output, so every point moves halfway toward the $x$-axis while keeping its $x$-coordinate. That is a vertical shrink, not a horizontal one.
steps: $\frac{1}{2}$ is outside the function, so the effect is vertical.
That is a vertical shrink by a factor of $\frac{1}{2}$.
problems.verify: result = "A vertical shrink by a factor of $\frac{1}{2}$."

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the line $y=2x+c$ intersects the parabola $y=x^{2}+6x+11$ at exactly one point, where $c$ is a constant. What is the value of $c$?
problems.solution: Exactly one intersection point means the quadratic left after substitution has a repeated root, so its discriminant is zero. Solving that equation for $c$ is the whole problem.
problems.verify:
c = symbols('c')
result = solve(16 - 4*(11 - c), c)[0]

problems.stem: How many solutions does the system of equations $y=x^{2}-6x+9$ and $y=x-3$ have?
problems.solution: Even though the parabola is a perfect square and the line passes through its vertex region, the combined quadratic has a positive discriminant, so the line cuts the curve twice.
steps: Discriminant: $49-48=1>0$, so there are two real solutions ($x=3$ and $x=4$).
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x', real=True)
result = len(solve(x**2 - 6*x + 9 - (x - 3), x))

problems.solution: Do the inside first: $g(5)$ needs $f(5-2)=f(3)$, and only then add the $3$ that sits outside. Reading $f(7)$ (shifting the wrong way) or forgetting the $+3$ are the two failures this item checks.

problems.stem: Which transformation takes the graph of $y=x^{2}$ to the graph of $y=-(x-2)^{2}$?
choices: A reflection across the $x$-axis and a shift $2$ units to the left.
A reflection across the $x$-axis and a shift $2$ units to the right.
A reflection across the $y$-axis and a shift $2$ units to the right.
A reflection across the $y$-axis and a shift $2$ units to the left.
problems.solution: The minus sign is outside the square, so it reflects the parabola across the $x$-axis. The $-2$ is inside, so it is horizontal and moves the graph in the opposite direction from its sign: $2$ units right.
steps: $-(\,\cdot\,)$ outside negates every output: reflection across the $x$-axis.
$x-2$ inside shifts the graph $2$ units right (the vertex needs $x-2=0$).
The new vertex is $(2,0)$ and the parabola opens downward.
problems.verify: result = "A reflection across the $x$-axis and a shift $2$ units to the right."

problems.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=(x+1)^{2}$. The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shifted $3$ units to the right. Which equation represents the resulting graph?
problems.solution: A shift $3$ units right replaces $x$ by $x-3$ in the formula: $f(x-3)=((x-3)+1)^{2}=(x-2)^{2}$. Replacing $x$ by $x+3$ --- shifting the wrong way --- gives $(x+4)^{2}$, which is the distractor to avoid.
steps: A right shift of $3$ means evaluating $f(x-3)$.

problems.stem: The function $f$ is defined by $f(x)=x^{2}-16$, and $g$ is defined by $g(x)=f\left(\frac{x}{2}\right)$. What is the positive $x$-intercept of the graph of $y=g(x)$?
problems.solution: Dividing the input by $2$ stretches the graph horizontally by a factor of $2$, so each $x$-intercept moves twice as far from the $y$-axis. The stretch acts on $x$, never on the outputs.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
result = max(solve((x/2)**2 - 16, x))

problems.stem: $$y=x^{2}+5x+4$$ $$y=3x+7$$ The system above has two solutions. What is the sum of the $y$-coordinates of the two solutions?
problems.solution: Substituting the line into the parabola gives the $x$-values; the line then converts each one to a $y$-value in a single step. Reporting only one point's $y$-value, or the sum of the $x$-values, are the two traps.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
xs = solve(x**2 + 5*x + 4 - (3*x + 7), x)
result = sum([3*v + 7 for v in xs])

problems.stem: The function $g$ is defined by $g(x)=-f(-x)$. Which of the following describes the graph of $y=g(x)$ in terms of the graph of $y=f(x)$?
choices: The graph of $f$ reflected across both the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis.
The graph of $f$ reflected across the $x$-axis only.
The graph of $f$ reflected across the $y$-axis only.
The graph of $f$ reflected across the line $y=x$.
problems.solution: There are two independent sign changes: the inner $-x$ reflects the graph across the $y$-axis, and the outer minus sign reflects it across the $x$-axis. Applying both is the same as rotating the graph $180^\circ$ about the origin.
steps: The leading minus sign then reflects that result across the $x$-axis.
A point $(a,b)$ on $f$ ends up at $(-a,-b)$.
problems.verify: result = "The graph of $f$ reflected across both the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis."

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, at how many points does the graph of $x^{2}+y^{2}=16$ intersect the graph of $y=x^{2}-4$?
problems.solution: Here it is cleaner to eliminate $x^{2}$ rather than $y$: the parabola gives $x^{2}=y+4$, which turns the circle equation into a quadratic in $y$. Each $y$-value must then be checked for how many $x$-values it produces --- one of them yields a single point, not two.
steps: $y=3$ gives $x^{2}=7$, two points; $y=-4$ gives $x^{2}=0$, one point.
In total there are $3$ intersection points.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y', real=True)
result = len(solve([x**2 + y**2 - 16, y - (x**2 - 4)], [x, y]))

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the line $y=kx$ is tangent to the graph of $y=x^{2}-2x+4$, where $k$ is a positive constant. What is the value of $k$?
problems.solution: Substituting gives $x^{2}-(2+k)x+4=0$, and tangency forces its discriminant to zero. That yields $(2+k)^{2}=16$, whose two roots are $k=2$ and $k=-6$; only the positive one is wanted.
problems.verify:
k = symbols('k')
result = max(solve((2 + k)**2 - 16, k))

problems.stem: The graph of $y=f(x)$ is shown, where $f(x)=(x-2)^{2}-1$. What is the vertex of the graph of $y=f(x+1)-2$?
problems.solution: Two transformations, read separately: $x+1$ inside moves the graph $1$ unit \emph{left}, and $-2$ outside moves it $2$ units down. The vertex $(2,-1)$ therefore lands at $(1,-3)$.
steps: From the graph, the vertex of $f$ is $(2,-1)$.
$f(x+1)$ shifts the graph $1$ unit left: the vertex $x$-coordinate becomes $2-1=1$.
problems.verify:
x = symbols('x')
h = (x - 1)**2 - 3
xv = solve(sp.diff(h, x), x)[0]
result = (xv, h.subs(x, xv))

problems.solution: Work from the inside out: the input $2$ becomes $2+1=3$ before $f$ is applied, and only the result is doubled. The factor $2$ multiplies the output, so it can never change which row of the table you read.

problems.stem: Which sequence of transformations takes the graph of $y=x^{2}$ to the graph of $y=2(x+3)^{2}$?
choices: A vertical stretch by a factor of $2$ and a shift $3$ units to the right.
A vertical stretch by a factor of $2$ and a shift $3$ units to the left.
A horizontal stretch by a factor of $2$ and a shift $3$ units to the left.
A shift $3$ units to the left and $2$ units up.
problems.solution: The $2$ multiplies the output, so it is a vertical stretch; the $+3$ lives inside the square, so it is a horizontal shift in the opposite direction --- $3$ units left. Mixing up which variable the $2$ acts on, or shifting right, are the intended errors.
steps: $2\cdot(\,\cdot\,)$ outside: vertical stretch by a factor of $2$.
$x+3$ inside: horizontal shift $3$ units left, since the vertex needs $x=-3$.
The vertex of the image is $(-3,0)$ and the parabola is twice as steep.
problems.verify: result = "A vertical stretch by a factor of $2$ and a shift $3$ units to the left."

problems.stem: In the $xy$-plane, the graph of $x^{2}+y^{2}=25$ and the graph of $y=x^{2}-13$ intersect at how many points?
problems.solution: Eliminating $x^{2}$ turns the system into a quadratic in $y$. Each admissible $y$ must then be traced back: here both $y$-values give a positive $x^{2}$, so each contributes two points.
problems.verify:
x, y = symbols('x y', real=True)
result = len(solve([x**2 + y**2 - 25, y - (x**2 - 13)], [x, y]))

problems.stem: $$y=x^{2}-2x+c$$ $$y=2x-5$$ In the system of equations above, $c$ is a constant. For what value of $c$ does the system have exactly one real solution?
problems.solution: Substituting leaves $x^{2}-4x+(c+5)=0$, and \emph{exactly one} real solution means a discriminant of zero. Note the $+5$: moving $-5$ across the equals sign is where the arithmetic usually goes wrong.
problems.verify:
c = symbols('c')
result = solve(16 - 4*(c + 5), c)[0]
